statement: Aging can be organized into nine interconnected cellular/molecular hallmarks: genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem-cell exhaustion, and altered intercellular communication.
effect_size: Framework (9 hallmarks); each must be measurable, aggravate aging when worsened, and ameliorate aging when reversed.

provenance.primary: López-Otín, Blasco, Partridge, Serrano, Kroemer — 'The Hallmarks of Aging', Cell 2013

confidence_notes: Organizing taxonomy, not a causal proof; modeled on Hanahan & Weinberg's Hallmarks of Cancer. ~15k citations.

statement: The hallmarks framework was expanded to twelve: the original nine plus disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation (inflammaging), and dysbiosis. Hallmarks are grouped as primary (causes of damage), antagonistic (responses that become deleterious), and integrative (culprits of phenotype).
effect_size: Framework (12 hallmarks, 3 categories).

provenance.primary: López-Otín, Blasco, Partridge, Serrano, Kroemer — 'Hallmarks of aging: an expanding universe', Cell 2023

confidence_notes: Update/expansion of the 2013 taxonomy; remains a conceptual map, not a unified mechanism.

statement: Rapamycin (mTOR inhibitor) fed from late life (600 days) extends median and maximal lifespan in genetically heterogeneous mice in both sexes.
effect_size: Median lifespan +9% (males) / +14% (females); first drug to extend mammalian lifespan started late in life.
population: Genetically heterogeneous (UM-HET3) mice, NIA ITP, 3 sites

provenance.primary: Harrison, Strong, Sharp et al. — Nature 2009

confidence_notes: Robust, replicated across the NIA Interventions Testing Program. Mouse outcome — NOT a demonstrated human lifespan effect.

statement: mTORC1 is a central nutrient/growth sensor; chronic mTORC1 activation suppresses autophagy and drives anabolic, pro-aging programs. Inhibiting it phenocopies aspects of caloric restriction.
effect_size: Pathway-level mechanism.

provenance.primary: Panwar et al. (review) — Signal Transduct Target Ther 2023; orig. concept Kaeberlein/Kennedy

confidence_notes: Mechanism claim only — do not read as a human outcome.

statement: AMPK is an energy-sensing kinase activated by rising AMP:ATP (low energy); it restores energy homeostasis and is a proposed mediator of CR/metformin/exercise longevity effects.
effect_size: Pathway mechanism.

provenance.primary: Hardie, Ross, Hawley — 'AMPK: a nutrient and energy sensor', Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 2012

confidence_notes: Mechanism; links metabolism to aging but human longevity outcome is inferential.

statement: Low-dose mTOR inhibition (RAD001/everolimus) for 6 weeks improved the antibody response to influenza vaccine in elderly humans (a healthspan-relevant surrogate of immunosenescence).
effect_size: ~20% increase in vaccine antibody titers vs placebo.

provenance.primary: Mannick et al. — 'mTOR inhibition improves immune function in the elderly', Sci Transl Med 2014

confidence_notes: Human RCT but the OUTCOME is an immune surrogate (vaccine response), NOT lifespan or disease endpoints.

statement: Sirtuins (NAD+-dependent deacylases, esp. SIRT1/SIRT3/SIRT6) regulate metabolism and genome maintenance; tissue NAD+ levels decline with age, reducing sirtuin activity.
effect_size: Age-associated NAD+ decline; SIRT6 OE extends male mouse lifespan (Kanfi 2012).

provenance.primary: Imai & Guarente (sirtuin/NAD axis reviews); Kanfi 2012 Nature for SIRT6

confidence_notes: Mechanistic. The resveratrol→SIRT1 activation story is contested (see CONFLICTS).

statement: Oral nicotinamide riboside (NR) is well tolerated and raises blood NAD+ ~40-60% in healthy middle-aged/older humans; it modestly reduced blood pressure/arterial stiffness in a pilot but has NOT shown disease or longevity outcomes.
effect_size: NAD+ ~+60%; BP signal exploratory and unconfirmed; no hard outcomes.

provenance.primary: Martens et al. — Nat Commun 2018 (9:1286)

confidence_notes: Surrogate (NAD+ level) is proven; clinical OUTCOME is not. Heavily marketed beyond the evidence.

statement: Reducing insulin/IGF-1-like signaling (daf-2 mutation) doubles lifespan in C. elegans via the FOXO transcription factor daf-16; this established nutrient-sensing/IIS as a conserved longevity lever.
effect_size: ~2x lifespan extension in worms.

provenance.primary: Kenyon, Chang, Gensch, Rudner, Tabtiang — 'A C. elegans mutant that lives twice as long as wild type', Nature 1993

confidence_notes: Foundational invertebrate genetics. Worm outcome; mammalian translation is partial (IGF-1 tradeoffs).

statement: Senescent cells (irreversible cell-cycle arrest with a pro-inflammatory SASP) accumulate with age and in age-related disease, contributing to tissue dysfunction and chronic inflammation.
effect_size: SASP-driven paracrine damage.

provenance.primary: Hernandez-Segura, Nehme, Demaria — 'Hallmarks of Cellular Senescence', Trends Cell Biol 2018

confidence_notes: Mechanism. Senescence is also anti-cancer/wound-healing — context-dependent, not purely harmful.

statement: Genetic clearance of p16Ink4a-positive senescent cells delays the onset of age-related pathologies (in a progeroid BubR1 model and, later, in naturally aged mice).
effect_size: Delayed sarcopenia, cataract, adipose loss; (2016) extended median lifespan ~25-27% in naturally aged mice.

provenance.primary: Baker et al. — Nature 2011 (10.1038/nature10600) and Baker et al. — Nature 2016

confidence_notes: Proof-of-concept that senescent cells are causal in mice. Genetic ablation tool, not a drug.

statement: Dasatinib + quercetin (D+Q) was identified as the first senolytic combination by targeting pro-survival 'SCAP' networks that senescent cells depend on, selectively killing them in vitro and in mice.
effect_size: Selective senescent-cell apoptosis.
population: Human/mouse senescent cell assays + aged mice

provenance.primary: Zhu et al. — 'The Achilles' heel of senescent cells', Aging Cell 2015

confidence_notes: Discovery/mechanism. Not a human outcome.

statement: Intermittent senolytic treatment improved physical function and extended median post-treatment lifespan (~36%) in old mice, and alleviated dysfunction when senescent cells were transplanted into young mice.
effect_size: Post-treatment median lifespan +36%; improved gait/grip/endurance.

provenance.primary: Xu et al. — 'Senolytics improve physical function and increase lifespan in old age', Nat Med 2018

confidence_notes: Strong mouse outcome. Human lifespan effect NOT shown.

statement: The flavonoid fisetin acts as a senotherapeutic, reducing senescent-cell burden and extending median and maximum lifespan in mice even when started late in life.
effect_size: Reduced senescence markers; extended median+max lifespan.

provenance.primary: Yousefzadeh et al. — 'Fisetin is a senotherapeutic that extends health and lifespan', EBioMedicine 2018

confidence_notes: Mouse outcome; widely sold as a supplement on the strength of animal data.

statement: A first-in-human open-label pilot of D+Q in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (n=14) reported improved physical function (6-min walk, gait speed) over 3 weeks.
effect_size: Improved 6MWD/gait/chair-stand; no control arm, tiny n, short.

provenance.primary: Justice et al. — EBioMedicine 2019

confidence_notes: Earliest human senolytic signal but UNCONTROLLED pilot — do NOT treat as efficacy. Larger RCTs ongoing.

statement: Yeast genetic screens defined the essential autophagy (ATG) genes and the molecular machinery of macroautophagy — the regulated lysosomal self-digestion that recycles damaged components (Ohsumi, Nobel Prize 2016).
effect_size: Defined ~15 core ATG genes / autophagosome pathway.

provenance.primary: Tsukada & Ohsumi 1993; Mizushima (review) — Genes Dev 2007

confidence_notes: Mechanism. 2016 Nobel in Physiology/Medicine to Ohsumi.

statement: Macroautophagy declines with age; restoring autophagy (genetically, by CR, rapamycin, or spermidine) is required for many longevity interventions, and 'disabled macroautophagy' is a 2023 hallmark.
effect_size: Autophagy is necessary downstream of CR/rapamycin/spermidine for lifespan effects.

provenance.primary: López-Otín et al. 2023 (hallmark); spermidine: Eisenberg 2009

confidence_notes: Mechanism/animal. Human autophagy-induction outcomes not established.

statement: DNA-methylation levels at 353 CpG sites form a multi-tissue 'epigenetic clock' that predicts chronological age across human tissues with median error ~3.6 years.
effect_size: Multi-tissue age predictor; r~0.96, MAE ~3.6y.

provenance.primary: Horvath — 'DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types', Genome Biol 2013

confidence_notes: A biomarker/correlate of age — NOT proof methylation causes aging. First-gen clock trained on chronological age.

statement: PhenoAge, a second-generation epigenetic clock trained on a composite clinical phenotype, predicts all-cause mortality and healthspan better than chronological-age clocks.
effect_size: Each year of PhenoAge acceleration ~ +9% mortality hazard (cohort).

provenance.primary: Levine et al. — 'An epigenetic biomarker of aging for lifespan and healthspan', Aging 2018

confidence_notes: Predictive biomarker (association). Acceleration is associated with mortality — not shown to be modifiable→outcome.

statement: GrimAge, a methylation clock built on DNAm surrogates of plasma proteins and smoking-pack-years, strongly predicts time-to-death and time-to-disease.
effect_size: Strongest mortality prediction among DNAm clocks (cohort).

provenance.primary: Lu et al. — 'DNA methylation GrimAge strongly predicts lifespan and healthspan', Aging 2019

confidence_notes: Association/prediction. Best-performing clock for mortality, still observational.

statement: DunedinPACE estimates the RATE of biological aging (years of aging per calendar year) from a single methylation sample, trained on longitudinal multi-organ decline in the Dunedin birth cohort.
effect_size: Faster pace associated with morbidity, disability, mortality.

provenance.primary: Belsky et al. — 'DunedinPACE', eLife 2022

confidence_notes: Pace-of-aging biomarker; used as a surrogate endpoint in intervention trials but not validated to causally track interventions.

statement: Four transcription factors (Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc — 'Yamanaka factors') can reprogram differentiated somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells, resetting cellular identity and epigenetic age.
effect_size: Defined-factor reprogramming to pluripotency; resets DNAm age toward zero.

provenance.primary: Takahashi & Yamanaka — Cell 2006

confidence_notes: Foundational mechanism (2012 Nobel). Full reprogramming erases identity/causes teratomas — basis for PARTIAL reprogramming.

statement: Cyclic, partial expression of Yamanaka factors ameliorates age-associated hallmarks and extends lifespan in a progeroid (LAKI) mouse without full dedifferentiation.
effect_size: Extended lifespan in progeroid mice; improved tissue function in aged WT.

provenance.primary: Ocampo et al. — 'In Vivo Amelioration of Age-Associated Hallmarks by Partial Reprogramming', Cell 2016

confidence_notes: Animal proof-of-concept; progeroid model inflates effect. Teratoma/identity-loss risk is the central open hazard.

statement: Partial reprogramming with OSK (omitting c-Myc) restored youthful methylation patterns and regenerated optic-nerve axons, restoring vision in aged and glaucomatous mice — evidence that aging involves recoverable epigenetic information.
effect_size: Axon regeneration + visual-function recovery in aged/injured mouse retina.
population: Mouse retinal ganglion cells in vivo

provenance.primary: Lu, Brommer, Tian, Sinclair et al. — Nature 2020

confidence_notes: Supports the 'information theory of aging.' Animal/tissue-specific outcome; human application is early (Altos, NewLimit).

statement: Caloric restriction (20-40% without malnutrition) extends lifespan across yeast, worms, flies, and rodents and is the most reproducible non-genetic longevity intervention in short-lived species.
effect_size: Up to +50% lifespan in rodents; effect size strain/diet-dependent.

provenance.primary: de Cabo & Mattson (review) — NEJM 2019; Weindruch & Walford foundational

confidence_notes: Strong in short-lived animals; magnitude shrinks and reverses in some mouse strains (ITP/genetic-background dependent).

statement: In the Wisconsin (WNPRC) rhesus-monkey CR study, calorie restriction delayed disease onset and reduced age-related and all-cause mortality.
effect_size: Reduced age-related death (HR favoring CR); less diabetes, cancer, CVD, brain atrophy.

provenance.primary: Colman et al. — Science 2009 (10.1126/science.1173635) & Nat Commun 2014

confidence_notes: Primate outcome — but CONFLICTS with the NIA study; difference largely attributed to control-diet quality and onset age.

statement: In the parallel NIA rhesus-monkey CR study, calorie restriction improved several healthspan markers but did NOT significantly extend survival overall.
effect_size: No significant survival benefit overall; metabolic improvements present.

provenance.primary: Mattison et al. — Nature 2012

confidence_notes: The famous null primate result. Control monkeys were fed less/healthier than Wisconsin controls.

statement: A joint re-analysis of both rhesus studies concluded CR does benefit primate health/survival, with discrepancies explained by age of onset, diet composition, sex, and feeding of controls.
effect_size: Adult-onset CR benefits survival; juvenile-onset and ad-lib-control design altered results.

provenance.primary: Mattison, Colman et al. — 'Caloric restriction improves health and survival of rhesus monkeys', Nat Commun 2017

confidence_notes: Partial reconciliation; underlines that CR outcome is context-dependent, not universal.

statement: In CALERIE-2, ~25% (achieved ~12%) calorie restriction for 2 years in healthy non-obese humans improved cardiometabolic risk markers and slowed the pace of aging (DunedinPACE) — but used surrogate, not mortality, endpoints.
effect_size: Improved LDL, BP, CRP, insulin sensitivity; ~2-3% slower DunedinPACE.

provenance.primary: Ravussin et al. 2015 (CALERIE); Waziry et al. Nat Aging 2023 (DunedinPACE re-analysis)

confidence_notes: Best human CR RCT. OUTCOME is biomarker/surrogate; long-term mortality effect unknown.

statement: Intermittent fasting / time-restricted regimens trigger a metabolic switch to ketone-body fuel and engage stress-resistance, autophagy and circadian pathways; human trials show metabolic benefits but disease/longevity outcomes remain mixed.
effect_size: Ketogenic switch + autophagy; weight/metabolic benefit ≈ caloric restriction in many trials.

provenance.primary: de Cabo & Mattson — 'Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Health, Aging, and Disease', NEJM 2019

confidence_notes: Mechanism + modest human metabolic outcomes. Much popular benefit may reduce to caloric/weight effects.

statement: Mitochondrial dysfunction — reduced bioenergetic efficiency, increased ROS leak, and impaired mitophagy/biogenesis — is a core aging hallmark linking metabolism, redox state and senescence.
effect_size: Bioenergetic decline + ROS; mitohormesis (low ROS can be beneficial).

provenance.primary: López-Otín et al. 2013/2023; Sun, Sadighi Akha, Wallace

confidence_notes: MECHANISM and a key UP-link to biophysics canon. The simple 'free-radical theory' is contested (see CONFLICTS).

statement: 'Inflammaging' — chronic, sterile, low-grade systemic inflammation — rises with age and predicts frailty, multimorbidity and mortality; it is now a recognized aging hallmark.
effect_size: Elevated IL-6/CRP/TNF predict mortality and frailty in elderly cohorts.

provenance.primary: Franceschi et al. (inflammaging); López-Otín 2023 (hallmark)

confidence_notes: Cohort-level association of inflammatory markers with outcomes; causality vs. consequence is debated.

statement: Telomeres shorten with cell division and age; critically short telomeres trigger senescence/apoptosis. Short leukocyte telomere length is associated with mortality, though effect sizes are modest and confounded.
effect_size: Short LTL associated with higher mortality (modest HR); Mendelian-randomization signals are mixed/bidirectional with cancer.

provenance.primary: López-Otín 2013 (hallmark); Blackburn/Epel telomere biology

confidence_notes: Hallmark mechanism is solid; the LTL-as-biomarker outcome is weaker/confounded than popular framing.

statement: Specific FOXO3A genotypes are strongly and reproducibly associated with human longevity across multiple ethnic populations — the most replicated longevity gene after APOE.
effect_size: OR ~1.3-1.5 for reaching extreme old age (per allele/genotype, varies).
population: Centenarian vs control cohorts (Hawaii, German, Italian, Japanese, etc.)

provenance.primary: Willcox et al. — 'FOXO3A genotype is strongly associated with human longevity', PNAS 2008

confidence_notes: Genetic ASSOCIATION (case-control/GWAS), not causal/interventional. FOXO3 = human ortholog of worm daf-16.

statement: APOE is the most consistent genetic locus affecting human lifespan: the ε4 allele shortens lifespan and raises Alzheimer's/CVD risk, while ε2 is associated with longevity.
effect_size: ε4 carriers reduced odds of longevity; ε2 enriched in centenarians (GWAS-significant).

provenance.primary: Deelen et al. 2019 (longevity GWAS); Sebastiani/Perls centenarian studies

confidence_notes: Robust association from GWAS; APOE and FOXO3 are the only loci replicated across most longevity GWAS.

statement: Extreme human longevity is highly polygenic with small per-variant effects; genome-wide longevity GWAS reliably implicate APOE and FOXO3 but most other hits are non-replicating, and heritability of lifespan is modest (~10-25%).
effect_size: Lifespan heritability ~10-25%; few robust loci beyond APOE/FOXO3.

provenance.primary: Deelen et al., Nat Commun 2019; Timmers et al. (parental lifespan)

confidence_notes: Tempers gene-hype: most longevity is environmental/stochastic, not a few 'longevity genes'.

statement: Type-2 diabetics initiated on metformin monotherapy showed lower all-cause mortality than matched non-diabetic controls in one large observational analysis — the headline rationale for testing metformin as a geroprotector.
effect_size: Metformin initiators ~survived longer than matched non-diabetic controls (observational).
population: ~180k UK CPRD records (diabetic vs matched non-diabetic)

provenance.primary: Bannister et al. — Diabetes Obes Metab 2014

confidence_notes: Observational and confounded (prevalent-user/immortal-time concerns); later analyses (e.g., MILES) are equivocal. NOT proof metformin slows aging.

statement: TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin) is a proposed multi-center RCT designed to test whether metformin delays a composite of age-related diseases — built primarily to establish 'aging' as a regulatory endpoint with the FDA.
effect_size: Design: ~3000 elderly, composite morbidity/mortality endpoint; not yet fully funded/completed as of 2026.

provenance.primary: Barzilai et al. — Cell Metab 2016 (TAME rationale)

confidence_notes: PROTOCOL/design, not a result. Its real target is the regulatory precedent, not a single drug.
